extracted.intended_audience: general readers and researchers interested in Scottish comedy (fans, students, cultural commentators)
extracted.subtask_description: Overview and descriptive criteria for the character and forms of comedy originating in Scotland, including tonal features, language use, recurring themes, and common media formats. Useful for readers analyzing or producing Scottish-flavoured humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone: 'cheeky rather than edgy'
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy in Scotland is described as 'cheeky rather than edgy', largely in part due to its use of language and innuendos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor a mischievous, playful tone over overtly confrontational or boundary-pushing 'edgy' material. Use wordplay and suggestive humor that feels teasing rather than aggressively transgressive. Example: the article explicitly characterizes Scottish comedy as 'cheeky rather than edgy.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of language and innuendo
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic tone is 'largely in part due to its use of language and innuendos.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage regional dialects, double entendres, and culturally-specific phrases (including Scots) to create humor. Innuendo and linguistic play are central tools; ensure audience comprehension or provide context when exporting material internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Scots and regional speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Scottish comedians 'gained an international audience during the 1960s–1970s, often sharing jokes in Scots', indicating language choice is a key element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate Scots vocabulary, pronunciations, and idioms to ground jokes in Scottish identity and flavor. When aiming for broader audiences, balance dialect authenticity with intelligibility or translate punchlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecation / mockery of national life
rubrics_metrics.description: Scottish comedians often display 'mockery of Scotland and Scottish culture' and the ability of Scottish people to 'laugh at themselves' is highlighted as a strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ self-deprecating humor and satire directed at local customs, institutions, and stereotypes. This inward-facing mockery can make material relatable and endearing to domestic audiences; be mindful of punching-up vs punching-down dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crudeness as a stylistic element
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy performances 'often sharing jokes in Scots with a sense of crudeness and mockery of Scotland and Scottish culture.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Crude or coarse elements (language, subject matter) are part of the tradition; use them deliberately to support character and tone, but consider broadcast standards and audience sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire aimed at Scottish life and institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted performers (e.g., Craig Ferguson) included 'satire jokes aimed at Scotland, Scottish culture and Scottish life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Target local institutions, social norms, and national identity for satirical commentary. Satire can be combined with self-deprecation to critique while maintaining affection for the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and broadcast constraints (watershed placement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Shows such as Still Game and Scot Squad are only shown on television channels, such as BBC Scotland, past the watershed due to its content of comedy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing material for television, account for scheduling and content-rating constraints — adult-oriented or explicit material may require late-night slots (post-watershed). Adjust language and themes according to platform and time-slot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-format presence (stand-up, sketch, television, film)
rubrics_metrics.description: Scottish comedy appears across television series, sketch shows, stand‑up, and film (the article lists TV comedies, sketch shows, stand-up comedians, and television/film comedians).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor comedic material to the conventions of the chosen format: tight setups for television sitcoms, rapid bits for sketches, personal storytelling for stand-up, and visual gags for film/TV. Examples in the article (Still Game, Chewin' the Fat, Limmy's Show) illustrate multiple successful formats.

rubrics_metrics.name: International appeal and portability
rubrics_metrics.description: The country has produced a number of comedians who have gathered an international audience; figures like Billy Connolly and Craig Ferguson became known internationally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To achieve cross-border success, combine distinctive local voice with universal themes (relationships, family, work) or translate culturally specific material into broadly relatable premises. Note examples: Connolly and Ferguson adapted Scottish-inflected comedy for international audiences.
